BGA and area-array rework · remove, reball, place and solder in one station

Ball grid arrays fail where nobody can see them. The SM-650 takes them off and puts them back.

The SM-650 is a single-station BGA rework system that combines a stepper-driven hot air head, a placement head and an optical vision system over an infrared preheat bed. Boards up to 550 x 500 mm are clamped in a laser-aligned fixture, heated through an eight-stage programmable profile with three independently controlled zones, and the component is removed, realigned and re-soldered without leaving the platform.

01 — Why this machine exists

A ball grid array gives you no second look

Every other component on a board can be inspected, touched up and re-inspected. A BGA hides all of its joints underneath itself. By the time the fault shows up in test, the board has already absorbed the full cost of every part and process that went into it — and the joints you cannot see are the ones deciding whether it ships.

The fault surfaces at the end of the line

A BGA that did not reflow properly, a void that grew during the second pass, a cracked ball from handling — none of it is visible from the top. It appears as an intermittent failure at functional test, or as a field return months later, when the board is at its most expensive and the diagnosis is at its hardest.

Scrapping is not the only cost

The board value is the obvious loss. The harder losses are the reflow oven slot spent on a board that never ships, the test time consumed proving a failure you already suspect, and the schedule slip when a customer build is waiting on a replacement board that has to be re-ordered, re-kitted and re-run.

Capability changes the decision

With a controlled rework station on the floor, a failed BGA becomes a task instead of a write-off. The board goes back through a measured thermal profile, the component is replaced or reballed, and the assembly returns to test. What changes is not only the yield figure — it is who gets to decide whether a board is recoverable.

Scope note: BGA rework is a controlled process, not a repair shortcut. Every profile on this page has to be validated on your own board, your own component and your own solder alloy before it is used in production. The machine supplies the control; your process engineer supplies the numbers.

02 — The process

Five stages, one clamped board, no re-fixturing

The operation manual issued with the machine describes four operating modes — Manual, Solder, Remove and Mount — that run on the same platform and the same clamped board. Between removing a failed device and soldering its replacement, the board never leaves the fixture and never loses its alignment reference.

Clamp and reference

Switch on the laser, move the chip to the centre of the red dot, then release the knobs, position the bracket, fix the PCB and tighten. The laser gives every subsequent step the same origin point.

Remove

In Remove mode, select the stored profile and start. The hot air head lifts the failed device on a controlled thermal ramp instead of a hand-held heat gun.

Clean the site

Clear the residual solder from the pads and prepare the land pattern for the replacement device, using the station's constant-temperature hold and vacuum functions.

Place

In Mount mode, start the profile and open the camera. Align the three red circles to the blue and yellow targets, turn the camera off and confirm — the nozzle then places the component.

Solder

In Solder mode, select the profile and start. The same eight-stage curve that removed the device reflows the replacement, and the cross-flow fan brings the board back down.

03 — The machine

Three heat zones, one optical axis, one control computer

The SM-650 integrates the hot air head and the placement head on a single stepper-driven carriage, so heating and placing happen on the same mechanical reference. Underneath, a large infrared preheat bed holds the whole board at a constant temperature while the heating plate is controlled independently.

What the introduction document states

  • Integrated hot air head and placement head, driven by stepper motor, with automatic soldering and automatic desoldering functions.
  • Up and down hot air with infrared at the bottom, independent heating in three temperature zones. Heating time and temperature are all displayed on the touch screen.
  • The upper heating head can be moved, which is convenient for manual operation.
  • The movable bottom has a large preheating area, and the PCB fixture can be adjusted flexibly on the X and Y axes, with a maximum splint size of 550 x 500 mm.
  • A powerful cross-flow fan at the bottom cools the assembly; temperature drops quickly and reliably.
  • Colour optical vision system with dichroic, magnifying and fine-tuning functions, including a colour-difference distinguishing device, automatic alignment focus and software operation. 27x optical zoom, maximum BGA size 70 x 70 mm that can be reworked.
  • Embedded industrial control computer, touch screen human-machine interface, PLC control, real-time temperature curve display. The fixed curve and the actual measured curve can be analysed against each other and compared with historical saved curves.
  • Built-in vacuum pump, 60 degree rotation, precise and fine-tuning mounting nozzle. Eight sections of rising or falling temperature plus eight sections of constant temperature control, with mass storage of temperature curves and on-screen curve analysis.

Two further points from the document belong here. The suction nozzle identifies its own suction and placement height automatically and holds pressure within a 30 to 50 gram window, which is what keeps a thin package from being crushed. And a BGA welding-zone support frame with fine-tunable height limits local sinking of the board under the heated area.

05 — Thermal control

The profile is the process. Everything else supports it.

On a BGA, the difference between a good joint and a failed one is not the peak temperature. It is the ramp, the soak, the time above liquidus and the way the board cools afterwards. The SM-650 stores the whole curve, not a single set point.

How the control layer works

  • Eight sections of rising or falling temperature plus eight sections of constant temperature control, so a full reflow curve can be built stage by stage.
  • Heating time and temperature for each stage are entered on the touch screen and displayed live during the run.
  • The real-time temperature curve is drawn against the programmed curve, so drift is visible while the board is still on the platform.
  • Measured curves can be compared with historical saved curves, which is how you prove a machine is still behaving the way it did when the profile was validated.
  • Profiles are stored by name, so a product can be recalled rather than re-entered — and an operator cannot silently invent a new curve.
  • A large infrared bed keeps the whole board at a constant temperature to prevent deformation, and the heating plate is controlled independently of it.

Three independent heating zones: up and down hot air with infrared at the bottom. The upper head is movable, which is what makes manual operation possible without dismantling the fixture.

06 — Capacity

The throughput maths, honestly

A rework station is a one-board-at-a-time tool. Its capacity is set by the thermal cycle, not by a conveyor speed, so the useful question is not how many boards an hour it can pass — it is how many boards a day it can recover without compromising the profile.

Cycle time is set by the curve

Removal, site cleaning, placement and re-soldering are four separate thermal and mechanical steps on the same board. Compressing them to hit a rate is exactly how a joint that looked good fails in the field. Plan the schedule around the validated profile, then decide how many boards fit a shift.

Plan around the worst board, not the average

A 70 x 70 mm package on a 550 x 500 mm board with a heavy copper plane takes longer to bring to temperature and longer to cool than a small package on a thin board. The station's cross-flow fan and independently controlled infrared bed are what keep that difference manageable rather than unpredictable.

Queue it like a machine, not like a bench

The workstation discipline that makes this pay is simple: one board in the fixture at a time, profiles stored by product name, and every rework logged against the board serial. That log is what turns rework from an anecdote into a yield figure you can act on.

We do not publish a boards-per-hour figure for this machine, because the source document does not state one and the real number depends entirely on your board, your package and your validated curve. Bring us a board and we will help you measure it.

10 — Insights

Eight short reads on rework that has to hold

These articles are written for the process engineer and the plant manager who own the yield number. Each one ends where it should: with something you can check on your own line.

Cost of quality

What one scrapped BGA board actually costs your plant

3 min read

A board that fails at functional test is never just the sum of its parts. By the time a BGA fault surfaces, that assembly has already been through printing, placement, reflow, possibly a second reflow, handling and test. Every one of those steps has been paid for, and none of it comes back.

Read the full article

The reason this is hard to manage is that the loss is spread across four budgets. Materials sit in one line. Oven and line time sit in another. Test engineering hours sit in a third. And the schedule slip — the customer build waiting on a replacement — sits nowhere at all, which is exactly why it gets ignored until it becomes a delivery problem.

A useful way to size it: count the boards that entered BGA rework or scrap in the last quarter, multiply by the finished board value, and then add the test hours spent proving each failure. That single number is usually the first honest estimate a plant has of what its BGA losses cost.

The reason to write the number down is that it converts a vague complaint into a decision. A plant that knows its annual BGA loss can compare it against the cost of a controlled rework station and see immediately which is larger — and that comparison is what actually releases the budget.

The ongoing value comes from logging. Once every rework is recorded against a board serial and a failure mode, the pattern stops being a surprise. You learn which product family fails, at which stage, and whether the cause was the process or the handling.

If you want to run that calculation properly, the payback panel on this page does it with your inputs. Bring the board count and the board value, and you will have the answer in about two minutes.

Thermal process

Reading a reflow profile the way the solder joint reads it

3 min read

A solder joint does not experience your set point. It experiences a history: how fast it was heated, how long it sat in the soak band, how far above liquidus it went, and how quickly it was pulled back down. Two machines set to the same peak can produce joints with completely different microstructures.

Read the full article

This is why hand rework is so difficult to control. A heat gun gives an operator one continuous feedback loop — the board in front of them — and no record of what the joint actually saw. When the board later fails, there is nothing to compare against, so the cause can only be guessed at.

The discipline that replaces it is straightforward. Build the curve in sections, run it identically every time, and keep the recorded measurement. On the SM-650 that means eight rising or falling sections plus eight constant-temperature sections, with the real-time curve drawn against the programmed one.

The comparison that matters most is not machine-to-spec. It is today's measured curve against the curve you saved on the day the profile was validated. A slow drift in a thermocouple or a heater does not announce itself — it shows up as a measured curve that no longer lies on top of the stored one.

That is the loop that keeps a rework process honest. Stored profiles mean an operator recalls a validated curve instead of inventing one; measured curves mean you can prove the machine is still behaving; and both together mean the process survives a shift change.

Start with one board, one component and one alloy. Instrument it, build the curve, and save it under a name that matches the product. Everything after that is repetition.

Process control

The eight-stage profile, explained stage by stage

4 min read

An eight-stage profile sounds like a technicality until you have to defend one in front of a customer's quality engineer. The reason the stages exist is that each one controls a different physical event, and skipping one does not shorten the cycle — it moves the risk somewhere you cannot see it.

Read the full article

The most common shortcut is the soak. Operators under time pressure reduce or remove it, because the board looks ready sooner. What the soak is doing is bringing the whole assembly — board, package and solder — to a uniform temperature before the peak, so the peak does not have to compensate for a cold plane underneath.

The SM-650 handles this with eight rising or falling sections and eight constant-temperature sections, each with its own time and temperature entered on the touch screen. That gives you the ability to shape the ramp and hold the soak without borrowing time from the peak.

Underneath all of it sits a large infrared preheat bed that holds the entire board at a constant temperature, with the heating plate controlled independently. This is the part that prevents the deformation you would otherwise get from heating a large board locally.

A BGA welding-zone support frame with fine-tunable height does the mechanical half of the same job, limiting local sinking of the board directly under the heated area. Thermal control and mechanical support are two halves of one problem.

The profiles are stored by name and can be recalled per product, which means the curve that was validated is the curve that runs. When measured curves are compared against saved historical curves, a change in machine behaviour becomes visible before it becomes a batch problem.

Write the profile down with the board construction, the alloy and the package it was validated for. A curve without that context is a number, not a process.

Vision and alignment

Why 27x optical zoom changes who can do BGA rework

3 min read

Placement accuracy on a fine-pitch BGA is not a matter of a steady hand. It is a matter of whether the operator can actually see the alignment target, and most rework benches answer that question badly.

Read the full article

The consequence of not seeing well is a placement that is close enough to reflow and wrong enough to fail later. Off by a fraction of a pad, the joint forms, passes a quick check, and then fails intermittently once the assembly sees thermal cycling in the field.

The SM-650 uses a colour optical vision system with dichroic, magnifying and fine-tuning functions, a colour-difference distinguishing device, automatic alignment focus and 27x optical zoom, with a maximum viewable area of 40 x 40 mm. In Mount mode the operator aligns three red circles to the blue and yellow targets, then turns the camera off and confirms.

The practical effect is that alignment becomes a procedure rather than a skill. The reference is on the screen, the targets either line up or they do not, and the decision does not depend on how many years the operator has been doing it.

That matters for shift coverage. A capability that lives in one experienced technician is a single point of failure for the whole rework process — it disappears on holiday, and it cannot be scaled by hiring.

Try this on your own bench: take your finest-pitch package and ask two different operators to align it, then inspect the result under X-ray. The variance between them is the number that tells you whether you need optics or a steadier hand.

Board handling

Keeping a 550 x 500 mm board flat while it is at 240 C

3 min read

Large boards do not fail uniformly. They bow, and the bow is worst in the middle, which is usually where the heaviest component sits. By the time the reflow peak arrives, the board has already moved.

Read the full article

The failure this produces is easy to misread. The joint looks fine immediately after rework and fails later, so the investigation goes looking for a solder problem when the actual cause was mechanical — a board that sank away from the nozzle at temperature.

The SM-650 addresses it from two directions at once. A large-scale infrared preheat bed holds the entire PCB at a constant temperature to prevent deformation, and the heating plate is independently controlled so the preheat does not have to be sacrificed to the profile.

Mechanically, a BGA welding-zone support frame with fine-tunable support height limits local sinking of the welding zone. The fixture itself is adjustable on the X and Y axes with a maximum splint size of 550 x 500 mm, and the maximum process area is 120 x 120 mm.

Handling matters too. The maximum board thickness the machine accepts is 4 mm, components up to 70 x 70 mm and 80 grams, and minimum spacing is 0.30 mm. Those limits are worth checking against your actual board before you plan a process around them.

The check is simple and worth doing before you buy anything: heat one of your largest boards in the fixture and watch the middle. If it moves, you need preheat and support, not a better nozzle.

Equipment planning

Rework station or rework line? Choosing by board mix

3 min read

The question that decides this is not volume. It is variety. A plant that reworks one product family with one package type can standardise far more aggressively than a plant that reworks whatever the customer mix delivers that week.

Read the full article

Plants get this wrong in both directions. Some buy a fully automatic line for a rework load that is genuinely intermittent, and then cannot justify it. Others buy a bench station for a load that needs repeatability and spend the next two years fighting variance.

The SM-650 is a single-station system with a specific envelope: boards up to 550 x 500 mm, components from 1 x 1 mm to 70 x 70 mm, up to 80 grams, minimum spacing 0.30 mm, maximum process area 120 x 120 mm. If your mix sits inside that envelope, one station can cover it.

What makes a station viable at that scale is repeatability rather than speed. Stored profiles, measured curve comparison, automatic suction and placement height detection, and pressure held within a 30 to 50 gram window are what let the same machine handle a fragile thin package and a heavy one without the operator relearning the job.

The machine is not trying to be a line. Machine size is 850 x 750 x 630 mm at approximately 80 kg on a single-phase 220 VAC supply, which means it goes onto an ordinary floor position rather than requiring a line installation.

Draw your last twelve months of rework onto two axes — package size and board size. If the dots cluster inside one rectangle, you have your answer, and it is usually a station.

Service and uptime

Spare parts, training and the first 30 days after installation

3 min read

A rework station earns its keep in the first month or it never does. What decides that is not the machine specification — it is whether the technician running it was trained on the actual board they have to rework.

Read the full article

Generic training is the usual failure. Someone learns the interface, returns to the plant, and then meets a board whose thermal mass behaves nothing like the training sample. The profile that worked in the demo does not work here, and confidence drops.

Southern Machinery lists four commitments with the machine: 7x24 worldwide support, free installation and training, a one-day lead time on spare parts, and a one-month window to develop a customised solution. The training is the one to schedule carefully.

The first thirty days should be structured around one product. Instrument a real board, build the profile, run it, inspect the result, and save the curve under that product's name. Repeat until two different operators can run it and get the same outcome.

The spare-parts lead time matters more than it looks. Consumables and wear items on a rework station — nozzles, thermocouples, the vacuum path — are what stop a validated process from running. A one-day lead time is the difference between a shift lost and a week lost.

Before you order, ask three questions: who trains the operator, on which board, and what happens when the first profile does not transfer. A supplier who answers those specifically is a supplier who has done this before.

Factory strategy

Where BGA rework capability fits a Smart EMS factory

4 min read

A Smart EMS factory is usually described in terms of what it automates: placement, inspection, transport, storage. Rework tends to sit outside that picture, treated as a manual exception rather than a process with data.

Read the full article

That framing has a cost. If rework is invisible in the data model, then the yield figure the factory reports is a yield-after-scrap figure, and the reason for the scrap never enters the improvement loop at all.

A controlled rework station changes that by producing a record. Profiles are stored by name, measured curves can be compared against historical saved curves, and each rework is a datable event against a board. That is enough to make rework part of the quality system instead of an exception to it.

It also changes the economics of the line upstream. A plant that can recover a board is a plant that can accept a tighter first-pass yield on a difficult new product, because the downside is bounded. That matters most during new product introduction, when processes are still being tuned.

On the sustainability side, recovering a populated board avoids re-manufacturing the whole assembly — the components, the laminates, the process energy and the logistics that went into it. Zero e-waste targets are easier to defend when the capability to recover exists on the floor.

The three independent heating zones, the infrared preheat bed and the stored profile library are what make that record trustworthy. Without thermal control, a rework log is just a note that someone tried.

If your factory reports a first-pass yield and a scrap cost, you already have the two numbers needed to size this. Put rework capability against them and see whether it moves.

13 — Questions

Answers to the questions this machine raises

These are the questions we are asked most often about the SM-650, answered from the source documents rather than from sales language.

What is the largest board the SM-650 can take?

550 x 500 mm, with a maximum board thickness of 4 mm. The maximum process area is 120 x 120 mm, so the heated and placed zone is smaller than the board itself — a large panel can be clamped and worked area by area.

What range of components can it rework?

From 1 x 1 mm to 70 x 70 mm, up to 80 grams in weight, with a minimum spacing of 0.30 mm. The document states that a maximum BGA size of 70 x 70 mm can be reworked.

What temperatures does it reach?

Maximum hot air temperature is 350 degrees Celsius and the infrared maximum is 400 degrees Celsius. Heating is split across three independent zones: hot air above and below, with infrared at the bottom. The upper heater is rated 1200 W, the lower heater 800 W and the bottom infrared board 3600 W.

How is the temperature profile controlled?

Through eight-stage programmable temperature settings. The control layer provides eight rising or falling sections plus eight constant-temperature sections, all entered on the touch screen, with the real-time curve displayed against the programmed curve and comparable with historical saved curves.

How accurate is the placement?

Placement uses a colour optical vision system with 27x optical zoom and a maximum viewing area of 40 x 40 mm, together with automatic alignment focus and a colour-difference distinguishing device. The suction nozzle identifies its own suction and placement height and holds pressure within a 30 to 50 gram window. The document does not state a placement tolerance in millimetres, so we do not quote one.

What does it need on site?

Single phase 220 VAC at 50 or 60 Hz. The machine measures 850 mm long, 750 mm wide and 630 mm high, and weighs approximately 80 kg. The document does not state a current draw — confirm the supply, breaker and earthing against your own site standard before ordering.

Does the board stay in the fixture between steps?

Yes. The operation manual describes four modes on one platform — Manual, Solder, Remove and Mount. The board is clamped once against a laser reference, and the removal, site cleaning, placement and re-soldering steps all run without re-fixturing.

Can you guarantee the profile will work on our board?

No, and no supplier honestly can. The recorded uniformity data on this page is a machine-capability measurement, not a production profile — the source document does not state which board, alloy or component was used. Your profile has to be validated on your own instrumented board before it is released to production. We will help you do that.
